newsitem.title: GERMANY: Continent greets Blair but sees slim impact on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Continent greets Blair but sees slim impact on EMU.

text.p: Continental Europe on Friday feted Tony Blair's resounding win in the British elections, but saw little hope that London would step effortlessly into line with its continental counterparts on Europe's monetary union.

Blair swept to power with a huge majority in Thursday's elections, seizing control from an embittered Conservative party which has all but torn itself apart in recent months over the thorny issue of Britain's participation in monetary union.
With EMU clearly an issue in the ballot boxes, big name Conservative euro-sceptics saw their majorities shrivel.

But as Blair himself avoids taking a long-term view on Britain's entry to monetary union, the results gave only limited comfort to those on the continent eager to welcome a full-qualified Britain into the single currency fold.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl, speaking in Brunei during an Asian tour, said the poll showed Britons did not like anti-European polemics and anti-EU policies could not win votes anywhere.

"Voters did not like the anti-European rhetoric of the past few days and weeks and this should be a lesson for all those who want to win votes with anti-European polemics," Kohl told reporters travelling with him.
But he urged Labour to come out much more strongly in favour of EMU, noting the stance had been cautious so far.
"I'm sure the new government will see very quickly and very clearly that standing on the sidelines amid all the developments in Europe will not bring any advantages for Britain," he said.
French president Jacques Chirac said he looked forward to a "confident dialogue" on Europe and other issues, but made no direct comment on Britain's EMU aims or chances.
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said simply that he was "convinced that Britain will be able to bring a determined contribution to the European integration process".
With even top politicians seemingly unclear on the new government's exact EMU aims, most analysts doubted a marked change in the "wait and see" stance was likely any time soon.
Philippe Brossard, Head of Research at ABN AMRO Finance in Paris, said: "It's slightly more favourable for the UK's participation (in EMU) although it remains very uncertain.

"It may change the overall EMU picture in the sense there is a bit less flexibility in the labour market and maybe more flexibity on deficits, pushing the overall balance towards a wider EMU, a weaker euro and a stronger dollar," he said.
Thomas Mayer at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt said: "From the German point of view Britain's stance on Europe is unlikely to change much in the foreseeable future.

"Politically, I cannot imagine that Tony Blair will want to pick up a hot potato like EMU which is even controversial within the ranks of his own party. If people expect Britain to stage a big swing towards EMU they will be disappointed."

Holger Schmieding, chief economist at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt, agreed: "In general, I don't think it means very much. Labour has turned a bit anti-European recently as well (as the Conservatives), so we'll really have to wait and see how this works out.

"Obviously Bonn and Paris are hoping that Blair will be more conciliatory towards Europe, but the question is whether he will be conciliatory not just in tone, but also in substance. For that, we might have to wait a while."

With the planned launch of the single currency now just 18 months away, Britain is seen having almost no chance of joining in the first round even if it wanted to, unless there were to be a delay in the 1999 start.

Even if it could argue its way out of a requirement for sterling to be in Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism for two years before the launch -- which it does not strictly meet -- poltical and technical issues could well prove a barrier.
Blair himself has stressed the "formidable obstacles" standing in the way of joining the single currency, making clear it is by no means certain that labour will sign up.
But analysts saw some benefits for EU cooperation in other areas, which could ultimately help the EMU case.

Adolf Rosenstock at Industrial Bank of Japan in Frankfurt said, "Britain's relation with the European Union will be more relaxed -- that should be the biggest benefit. But I doubt we'll see a more positive stance on European monetary union.
And Patrick Mange, economist at Deutsche Bank in Paris, said France could have a particular interest in persuading Britain to sign up for EMU soon.
"The French are more in favour of the UK participating than the Germans because they don't want a euro managed like the mark -- and the British don't want it either," he said.
